# Rocketwind — Tailwind-style CSS, generated by Go

If your Go app lets people build pages or edit their theme, the CSS you need
doesn't exist when you build the app. It depends on what someone saves tomorrow.

Rocketwind is being built to compile that CSS inside your Go process. No Node
process, no build step for each edit, and no need to ship every possible utility
class to every visitor.

**Work in progress.** Core utilities, variants, stylesheet directives and the
Go plugin API work, along with typed settings, named classes and the forms
plugin. The other standard plugins, CLI and compatibility profiles are still
being built.
See [WORK.md](WORK.md) for the implementation gates.


Why?
----

Three things that are awkward with a conventional CSS build:

* **Generate CSS on the fly.** A template, page builder or plugin introduces
  `grid-cols-3` after your binary has shipped. Compile what it uses when you load
  the template, and cache the result.
* **Give each account its own CSS.** Different organizations choose different
  colors, fonts, spacing and components. Compile a stylesheet for each account
  from its configuration, without rebuilding your application.
* **Let people edit settings.** A theme editor stores a heading size and a brand
  color. A component can say `text-{heading.size} bg-{brand.color}`. Your code
  supplies the values and their types; Rocketwind turns them into CSS for a
  named class such as `.signup-button`.

The last case matters because Tailwind's names can be ambiguous. `text-*` can
mean a font size or a color. A setting's type should settle that question even
when its value is a CSS variable. Rocketwind does not guess from its name.

Ordinary helper classes work too: pass in `text-xl`, `hover:flex` and the other
classes your templates use, and get a stylesheet back. Configuration can come
from Go; you don't need a single entry-point CSS file.

```go
compiler := rocketwind.New(rocketwind.Config{
    Theme: map[string]string{"--color-brand": "#663399"},
})
css, err := compiler.Build([]string{"grid", "p-4", "text-xl", "bg-brand"})
```

Or start with a stylesheet containing `@theme`, `@utility`, `@apply` and
`@tailwind utilities`, using `rocketwind.Compile(css, config)`. Imports can use
`Config.LoadStylesheet`; Go configuration and plugins use `Config.LoadModule`.
The standard Tailwind theme and preflight stylesheet are built in.

For configuration entirely in Go, `NewWithPlugins(config, plugins...)` runs
plugin callbacks before returning the compiler. `PluginAPI` registers base
styles, component selectors, static utilities, variants and typed functional
utilities with named values, fractions, modifiers and negative values.

`compiler.Parse(class)` exposes the parsed candidates, including explicit value
types. `compiler.Print(candidate)` produces their normalized spelling.

`Build` compiles exactly the classes passed to it; separate accounts do not
accumulate each other's classes. For a file watcher or a growing template set,
use `compiler.NewBuilder()`. Its `Build` method accumulates candidates, compiles
only additions, and returns cached CSS when nothing changed. `Reset` starts a
fresh stylesheet. Compilers and prepared templates can be shared across
goroutines; each incremental builder belongs to one caller.


Editable settings and named classes
----------------------------------

Prepare a class list once. Supply types now and values when an account's CSS is
needed:

```go
settings := map[string]rocketwind.ValueType{
    "heading.size": rocketwind.TypeLength,
    "brand.color":  rocketwind.TypeColor,
}
button, err := compiler.Prepare("text-{heading.size} bg-{brand.color}",
    rocketwind.TemplateOptions{
        TypeOf: func(name string) (rocketwind.ValueType, error) {
            return settings[name], nil
        },
    })
css, err = button.CSS(".signup-button", func(p rocketwind.Parameter) (rocketwind.Value, error) {
    return rocketwind.Value{CSS: accountSettings[p.Expression]}, nil
})
```

Rocketwind treats expressions such as `heading.size` as opaque strings. Your code
owns lookup, inheritance and validation. Values are literal CSS: underscores and
spaces are preserved. Set `Named: true` to supply a theme token such as `xl`
instead, or `Omit: true` to leave out a utility whose setting is unset.

A whole-class parameter, such as `hover:{button.styles}`, has type `TypeClasses`.
Return `Value{Classes: anotherTemplate}` to inline it. Its `Resolve` field can
supply a different resolver, preserving the scope where those classes were
defined. References inherit surrounding variants and `!`; cycles are errors.
Parameters also work inside arbitrary values and variants, for example
`w-[calc(100%_-_{gap})]` and `min-{breakpoint}:flex`.

Use `compiler.Render([]rocketwind.Rule{...})` to compile several named selectors
with one set of shared theme variables and property registrations. Named rules
preserve class-list order, so later declarations can override earlier ones.
Prepared templates can be reused concurrently with independent resolvers.

Older class spellings can opt into `Config.Aliases`. For example,
`"family": {Utility: "font", Type: rocketwind.TypeFamilyName}` makes `family-*`
mean a font family. Aliases do not change the default Tailwind vocabulary.
`TemplateOptions.DollarReferences` also accepts `$name` as shorthand for `{name}`.


Reuse existing CSS
------------------

If your application already ships a stylesheet, add only the helpers it lacks:

```go
existing, err := rocketwind.DefinedClasses(mainCSS, widgetsCSS)
compiler := rocketwind.New(rocketwind.Config{ExistingClasses: existing})
css, err := compiler.Build(templateClasses)
```

Class names are read from CSS selectors, including escaped names and nested
rules. Text inside comments, declarations, attributes, `:not()` and `:has()`
does not count as a class definition. Exclusion applies to generated helpers;
`@apply` and named rules still resolve those utilities. Imported stylesheets
must be passed separately. Rocketwind does not compare declaration values:
when a class already exists, the supplied stylesheet owns its behavior.


Standard plugins
----------------

`@tailwindcss/forms` **0.5.11** is built in. Use `@plugin "@tailwindcss/forms"`
in a stylesheet, with the same `strategy: "base"` or `strategy: "class"` option,
or pass `rocketwind.Forms(rocketwind.FormsOptions{})` to `NewWithPlugins`.
Its CSS matches 24 differential cases against the real plugin, plus 20 SVG
encoding cases. This upstream release contains no automated tests to import.
Typography and the remaining standard plugins are still in progress.


Tailwind compatibility
----------------------

| Version | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Tailwind CSS **4.3.4** | Current target. All 2,146 compiler calls captured from ten upstream suites match exactly, plus 6,151 syntax, normalization, CSS nesting and helper calls. The full upstream suite is not yet ported, so complete compatibility is not yet verified. |
| Tailwind CSS **3.4.17** | Planned compatibility profile for existing applications. Not yet implemented or verified. |

The goal is to reproduce the core compiler and standard plugins in Go, including
their upstream tests. Running JavaScript configuration or arbitrary JavaScript
plugins is outside the scope. Those extensions need Go implementations.

Version compatibility includes defaults and generated CSS, not just accepting
the same class names. An older application must be able to keep its existing
styles while adopting Rocketwind. New templates should be able to use the
current version. Utilities already supplied by another stylesheet must not be
generated twice.

The library currently has **zero dependencies**. JavaScript tools are used only
to run upstream tests and capture reference results during development.
